decks.title: Biotechnology: Principles and Processes — Part 1: Tools of recombinant DNA technology
goals: Define biotechnology and state its two core principles
Describe isolation of genomic DNA by cell lysis and separation of fragments by gel electrophoresis
Explain the discovery, naming and action of restriction enzymes and the role of ligase
State the features of a good cloning vector and describe pBR322, Ti plasmid, retroviruses, BAC and YAC

slides.heading: Biotechnology
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the tools used to cut, separate, join and carry genes.

nodes.label: Join into a vector with ligase

visual.alt: Flow from isolating DNA to cutting, separating and joining it into a vector

slides.narration: Biotechnology uses living organisms, cells or enzymes to make products and processes useful to humans. Its modern form depends on tools that let us take a gene out of one organism and put it into another.

slides.heading: Definition and principles
slides.body_md: The **European Federation of Biotechnology** defines biotechnology as the integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof and molecular analogues for products and services. Modern biotechnology rests on **two core techniques**.

rows: Alters the chemistry of DNA or RNA and introduces it into a host organism, changing its phenotype
Keeps sterile, contamination-free conditions so that only the desired microbe or cell grows in large quantities to make products such as antibiotics, vaccines and enzymes

visual.alt: Table of the two core principles of biotechnology

slides.narration: Genetic engineering creates the organism with the gene we want. Bioprocess engineering then grows it in huge, sterile vessels so that the product can be made on an industrial scale.

slides.heading: Isolating genomic DNA
slides.body_md: DNA lies inside membranes along with proteins, RNA and other molecules. It must be released and purified.

rows: Lysozyme for bacteria, cellulase for plant cells, chitinase for fungi
Chilled ethanol: DNA appears as fine threads, removed by spooling

visual.alt: Table of the steps of isolating genomic DNA

slides.narration: Each kind of cell wall needs its own enzyme. After lysis, enzymes digest the RNA and proteins, and cold ethanol makes the long DNA molecules come out of solution as fine white threads that can be wound onto a glass rod.

slides.heading: Gel electrophoresis
slides.body_md: DNA fragments are separated in **agarose gel** (a polysaccharide from seaweed). DNA is **negatively charged**, so in an electric field it moves towards the **anode (+)**. The gel acts as a **sieve**: **smaller fragments move farther**. Bands are stained with **ethidium bromide** and seen as **orange bands under UV light**, then cut out and **eluted**.

slides.narration: Fragments of known size, the ladder, are run beside the sample, so the size of each unknown band can be estimated by comparing positions. The band carrying the gene of interest is cut out and the DNA extracted for cloning.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: sizing fragments on a gel
slides.body_md: A ladder of 5000, 2000, 1000, 500, 200 and 100 bp is run beside a sample. The sample bands lie (i) between the 5000 and 2000 bands, (ii) between 1000 and 500, and (iii) between 200 and 100. Estimate each size range and say which moved farthest.
bullets: Compare each band with its neighbours in the ladder: (i) **2000–5000 bp**, (ii) **500–1000 bp**, (iii) **100–200 bp**.
Distances moved follow size: 4000 bp → 84 units; 600 bp → 133 units; 150 bp → 169 units.
Band (iii), the **smallest**, moved **farthest** towards the anode.

visual.alt: Worked table: sample bands of about 4000, 600 and 150 base pairs

slides.narration: Read each sample band against the ladder beside it. A band between the one thousand and five hundred markers must be between those sizes. The smallest fragment always travels farthest, because it slips most easily through the gel.

slides.heading: Restriction enzymes: discovery and naming
slides.body_md: In **1963**, two enzymes were found in **E. coli** that **restrict the growth of bacteriophages**: one adds **methyl groups** to DNA, the other **cuts** DNA — a **restriction endonuclease**. The first whose action depended on a **specific sequence**, **Hind II**, was isolated five years later; it cuts at a particular six-base-pair sequence.

rows: First enzyme isolated from this strain

visual.alt: Table explaining the name EcoRI

slides.narration: Restriction enzymes are molecular scissors. Exonucleases remove nucleotides from the ends of DNA, while endonucleases cut at specific positions within it. Their names record the bacterium they came from.

slides.heading: How EcoRI cuts DNA
slides.body_md: Each restriction endonuclease recognises a specific **palindromic** sequence — one that reads the **same 5′→3′ on both strands**. EcoRI cuts **GAATTC** between **G and A** on both strands, a little away from the centre, leaving single-stranded overhangs called **sticky ends**.

slides.narration: Sticky ends form hydrogen bonds with complementary sticky ends. If a vector and a foreign DNA are cut with the same enzyme, their sticky ends match, and the enzyme DNA ligase seals them together.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: cutting a sequence
slides.body_md: A top strand reads 5′–TTGAATTCCAGGCGAATTCTA–3′. EcoRI cuts between G and A of each GAATTC. How many fragments are formed, and what are their top-strand sequences? Is GAATTC a palindrome?
bullets: GAATTC occurs **2** times, so there are **3** fragments.
Fragments: **TTG | AATTCCAGGCG | AATTCTA**.
Reverse complement of GAATTC = GAATTC, so it is **palindromic**.

visual.alt: Worked table: 3 fragments

slides.narration: Find each recognition site, then cut after the G. Two sites in a linear molecule give three pieces. The same site read on the other strand, from five prime to three prime, is identical, which is what palindromic means for DNA.

slides.heading: Joining DNA and the steps of recombinant DNA technology
slides.body_md: **DNA ligase** joins the sugar–phosphate backbones of fragments with matching sticky ends, producing **recombinant DNA**.

visual.alt: Flow of the steps of recombinant DNA technology

slides.narration: The process runs from isolating DNA, through cutting and joining, to putting the recombinant DNA into a host and growing that host to make the desired product.

slides.heading: Quick check: isolating DNA
slides.body_md: What is added to make purified DNA come out of solution as fine threads?
slides.narration: Quick check. It is an alcohol, used very cold.

slides.heading: Features of a good cloning vector
slides.body_md: A **vector** carries foreign DNA into a host and multiplies there.

rows: Starts replication and controls the copy number of linked DNA
Lets transformants be picked out, for example genes for resistance to ampicillin or tetracycline
Single recognition sites for commonly used restriction enzymes, so the vector is cut only once
Easier to handle and to take up

visual.alt: Table of features of a good cloning vector

slides.narration: If a vector had several sites for one enzyme, cutting would break it into pieces. A single site, ideally inside a marker gene, makes the vector easy to open, join and select.

slides.heading: The plasmid pBR322
slides.body_md: **pBR322** is an **E. coli** plasmid vector with **ori**, the **rop** gene (for proteins involved in replication), and two antibiotic-resistance genes, **ampᴿ** and **tetᴿ**, carrying recognition sites such as **BamHI** (in tetᴿ), **PstI** and **PvuI** (in ampᴿ), and **EcoRI, HindIII, ClaI, SalI, PvuII**.

slides.heading: Other vectors
slides.body_md: Natural genetic engineers have been turned into vectors.

rows: Delivers DNA that transforms plant cells; disarmed so it no longer causes tumours
Insert their DNA into host chromosomes
Carries very large inserts in yeast

visual.alt: Table of other cloning vectors

slides.narration: Agrobacterium naturally moves a piece of its plasmid into plant cells and causes tumours. With the tumour genes removed, the plasmid can deliver useful genes instead. Retroviruses are disarmed in the same way for animal cells.

slides.heading: Quick check: ori
slides.body_md: Which part of a vector controls the copy number of linked DNA?
slides.narration: Quick check. It is where replication starts.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Biotechnology rests on genetic engineering and bioprocess engineering.
DNA isolation: lysozyme, cellulase or chitinase; ribonuclease; protease; chilled ethanol; spooling.
Gel electrophoresis: agarose; DNA moves to the anode; smaller fragments farther; ethidium bromide and UV; elution.
Restriction endonucleases (Hind II first; EcoRI named after E. coli RY 13) cut palindromes, leaving sticky ends; ligase joins.
Vector features: ori, selectable marker, single cloning sites; pBR322, Ti plasmid, retroviruses, BAC, YAC.

rows: Cuts DNA at a specific site

visual.alt: Summary table of enzymes and roles

slides.narration: To recap: DNA is isolated, cut by restriction enzymes at palindromic sites, separated on a gel, and joined into a vector by ligase. Good vectors have an origin of replication, a selectable marker and single cloning sites.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Explain each letter of **EcoRI**.
Draw **sticky ends** after an EcoRI cut.
Name the **enzyme for each cell wall** in DNA isolation.
Give the **role of ori, markers and cloning sites** with pBR322 examples.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Be ready to expand the name EcoRI letter by letter. Practise drawing sticky ends. Match each cell wall with the enzyme that breaks it. And explain each feature of a vector using pBR322.

decks.title: Biotechnology: Principles and Processes — Part 2: Getting genes into hosts and making products
goals: Describe how recombinant DNA is transferred into competent hosts
Explain selection of recombinants by antibiotic resistance, insertional inactivation and blue-white screening
Describe gene amplification by PCR and in vivo, and the use of bioreactors and downstream processing

slides.heading: From recombinant DNA to product
slides.body_md: Part 2 — putting recombinant DNA into cells, finding the right cells, copying genes and scaling up production.

visual.alt: Flow from transfer into host to selection, amplification and production

slides.narration: Once a gene is joined into a vector, it must enter a host, the host cells carrying it must be identified, the gene must be copied, and the product must be made on a large scale and purified.

slides.heading: Making host cells competent
slides.body_md: DNA is **hydrophilic** and cannot pass easily through cell membranes. Bacteria are made **competent** by treating them with a **divalent cation such as calcium**.

rows: Increases the efficiency with which DNA enters
Incubate cells with recombinant DNA on ice

visual.alt: Table of the steps of making bacteria competent

slides.narration: Calcium ions and a brief rise in temperature make the bacterial membrane let DNA in. Only a small fraction of cells take up the plasmid, so these must then be picked out.

slides.heading: Other methods of gene transfer
slides.body_md: Different hosts need different methods.

rows: DNA injected directly into the nucleus with a fine needle
Gold or tungsten particles coated with DNA are fired at high velocity
Agrobacterium or retroviruses deliver the gene

visual.alt: Table of methods of gene transfer

slides.narration: Plant cells have tough walls, so DNA-coated metal particles are shot into them with a gene gun. Animal cells can be injected directly. Disarmed Agrobacterium and retroviruses use their natural ability to deliver genes.

slides.heading: Selecting recombinants
slides.body_md: After transfer, only some cells are **transformants**, and only some of those carry **recombinant** DNA.

rows: On an ampicillin plate only cells with the plasmid (ampᴿ) grow
Foreign DNA inserted at the BamHI site inside tetᴿ destroys tetracycline resistance; recombinants grow on ampicillin but not on tetracycline
Insert placed inside lacZ; recombinant colonies cannot make β-galactosidase and stay white

visual.alt: Table of methods of selecting recombinants

slides.narration: Selection with two antibiotics is laborious, because cells must be plated on two kinds of medium. Insertional inactivation of a colour-producing gene lets recombinants be seen at a glance.

slides.heading: Blue-white selection
slides.body_md: The vector carries **lacZ**, coding for **β-galactosidase**. Colonies grown with a **chromogenic substrate** turn **blue** if the enzyme is made. Foreign DNA inserted **inside lacZ** inactivates it (**insertional inactivation**), so **recombinant colonies are white**.

slides.body_md: On the plate, 18 colonies are blue and 6 are white. Which are recombinant, and what percentage of the colonies is that?

Each cycle: **denaturation** (high temperature separates strands), **annealing** (two **primers** bind), and **extension** by a **thermostable DNA polymerase** isolated from **Thermus aquaticus** (**Taq polymerase**). Copies **double** every cycle.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: how many copies?
slides.body_md: A PCR starts with 4 copies of a target sequence. How many copies are there after 20 cycles, assuming perfect doubling?
bullets: That is about four million copies — enough to see on a gel or to clone.

slides.narration: Each cycle doubles the number, so twenty cycles multiply it by about a million. That is why PCR can work with the tiny amounts of DNA in a drop of blood or a single hair.

slides.heading: Amplification in vivo
slides.body_md: A gene can also be multiplied **in vivo** by **cloning**: the recombinant vector replicates inside the host, and the host multiplies.

rows: Set by ori of the vector

visual.alt: Table comparing PCR and in vivo amplification

slides.narration: In a living host, each cell can carry many copies of a high-copy plasmid, and the cells themselves divide. If the gene is expressed, the host also makes the protein, which is what industry usually wants.

slides.body_md: Two common designs differ in how they mix and aerate the culture.

Air through a sparger, spread by the stirrer
Sterile air bubbled through the medium
Larger surface area for oxygen transfer; no moving parts in the medium

slides.narration: Both designs aim to give every cell enough oxygen and nutrients. In a sparged tank, rising bubbles do the mixing; in a stirred tank, an impeller does.

sections.heading: 1. Principles; isolating DNA; gel electrophoresis
sections.body_md:
**Biotechnology** deals with techniques of using live organisms or enzymes from organisms to produce products and processes useful to humans. The **European Federation of Biotechnology (EFB)** defines it as “the integration of natural science and organisms, cells, parts thereof, and molecular analogues for products and services”.

**Two core techniques:** (i) **genetic engineering** — altering the chemistry of genetic material (DNA/RNA), introducing it into host organisms and thus changing their phenotype; (ii) **bioprocess engineering** — maintaining **sterile (microbial-contamination-free)** conditions to grow only the desired microbe or eukaryotic cell in large quantities to make antibiotics, vaccines, enzymes and other products.

**Isolation of genomic DNA:** cells are broken open with enzymes — **lysozyme** (bacteria), **cellulase** (plant cells), **chitinase** (fungi). **RNA** is removed with **ribonuclease** and **proteins** (such as histones) with **protease**. Addition of **chilled ethanol** precipitates purified DNA as a collection of **fine threads** in suspension, removed by **spooling**.

**Gel electrophoresis:** DNA fragments are separated in a matrix of **agarose**, a natural polymer extracted from **sea weeds**. DNA is **negatively charged** and moves towards the **anode** under an electric field. The gel acts as a **sieve**, so **smaller fragments move farther**. Separated DNA is stained with **ethidium bromide** and seen as bright **orange bands under UV** light. Bands are cut out and the DNA extracted (**elution**) for use in constructing recombinant DNA.

sections.heading: 2. Restriction enzymes and ligase
sections.body_md:
In **1963** two enzymes responsible for **restricting the growth of bacteriophage** in ***Escherichia coli*** were isolated: one **added methyl groups** to DNA, the other **cut DNA** (restriction endonuclease). The first restriction endonuclease whose action depended on a **specific DNA sequence**, **Hind II**, was isolated five years later; it always cuts DNA at a particular point by recognising a specific sequence of **six base pairs** (its recognition sequence). More than 900 restriction enzymes are now known from over 230 strains of bacteria.

**Nomenclature:** the first letter comes from the **genus** and the next two from the **species** of the prokaryote; the next letter is the **strain**, and the Roman numeral the **order of isolation**. **EcoRI**: ***E***scherichia ***co***li, strain ***R***Y 13, the first (***I***) enzyme.

**Features:** restriction enzymes belong to the **nucleases**. **Exonucleases** remove nucleotides from the ends of DNA; **endonucleases** cut at specific positions within it. Each restriction endonuclease recognises a specific **palindromic nucleotide sequence** — the sequence reads the **same on the two strands** when the orientation of reading is kept the same (5′→3′). They cut the strands **a little away from the centre** of the palindrome, between the same two bases on both strands, leaving **single-stranded overhangs** — **sticky ends**, which form hydrogen bonds with complementary cut counterparts. **DNA ligase** then joins the fragments. (Example: EcoRI cuts 5′–TTGAATTCCAGGCGAATTCTA–3′ into 3 fragments.)

**Steps of recombinant DNA technology:** isolation of DNA → fragmentation by restriction endonucleases → isolation of the desired DNA fragment → ligation into a vector → transfer of rDNA into a host → culturing host cells in a medium at large scale → extraction of the desired product.

sections.heading: 3. Cloning vectors
sections.body_md:
**Features required for cloning into a vector:**
- **Origin of replication (ori):** the sequence from where replication starts; any DNA linked to it can replicate in the host. It also controls the **copy number** of the linked DNA.
- **Selectable marker:** helps identify and eliminate **non-transformants** and selectively permit growth of **transformants** — normally genes encoding resistance to antibiotics such as **ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline or kanamycin**.
- **Cloning sites:** the vector should have **very few, preferably single**, recognition sites for commonly used restriction enzymes.
- **Small size** of the vector.

**pBR322** is an *E. coli* cloning vector with **ori**, **rop** (codes for proteins participating in plasmid replication), **ampᴿ** and **tetᴿ**, and restriction sites for **Hind III, EcoRI, BamHI, SalI, PvuII, PstI, ClaI** and **PvuI**; BamHI and SalI lie within **tetᴿ**, PvuI and PstI within **ampᴿ**.

**Vectors for plants and animals:** ***Agrobacterium tumefaciens***, a pathogen of dicots, delivers a piece of DNA (**T-DNA**) that transforms normal plant cells into a tumour; its **Ti plasmid** has been modified into a **non-pathogenic** cloning vector. **Retroviruses** in animals transform normal cells into cancerous ones; **disarmed retroviruses** are used to deliver desirable genes into animal cells. For very large DNA (genome projects), **BAC (bacterial artificial chromosome)** and **YAC (yeast artificial chromosome)** vectors are used.

sections.heading: 4. Transfer into hosts and selection of recombinants
sections.body_md:
**Competent host:** DNA is hydrophilic and cannot pass through cell membranes. Bacterial cells are made **competent** by treatment with a specific concentration of a **divalent cation such as calcium**. Recombinant DNA is incubated with the cells **on ice**, given a brief **heat shock at 42 °C**, and put **back on ice**, which enables the bacteria to take up the DNA.

**Other methods:** **microinjection** — recombinant DNA injected directly into the **nucleus of an animal cell**; **biolistics (gene gun)** — plant cells are bombarded with high-velocity micro-particles of **gold or tungsten coated with DNA**; **disarmed pathogen vectors** — Agrobacterium or retroviruses that transfer the recombinant DNA when they infect cells.

**Selection of recombinants:**
- **Antibiotic resistance:** when pBR322 carrying ampᴿ is introduced, only **transformants** grow on **ampicillin** medium.
- **Insertional inactivation of an antibiotic-resistance gene:** foreign DNA ligated at the **BamHI site of tetᴿ** destroys tetracycline resistance. Recombinants grow on **ampicillin** but **not on tetracycline**; non-recombinants grow on both. This needs simultaneous plating on two media.
- **Blue-white selection:** the foreign DNA is inserted within the coding sequence of **β-galactosidase (lacZ)**, inactivating it (**insertional inactivation**). On a medium with a **chromogenic substrate**, colonies **without** an insert make **blue** colonies; **recombinant** colonies remain **white**.

sections.heading: 5. Gene amplification
sections.body_md:
**Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)** — amplification **in vitro**. Multiple copies of the gene of interest are synthesised using **two sets of primers** (small chemically synthesised oligonucleotides complementary to the ends of the target region) and **DNA polymerase**. Each cycle has three steps:
1. **Denaturation** — high temperature separates the two strands.
2. **Annealing** — primers bind to the complementary regions.
3. **Extension** — the enzyme extends the primers using the nucleotides provided.
The **thermostable DNA polymerase** isolated from the bacterium ***Thermus aquaticus*** (**Taq polymerase**) remains active during the high-temperature denaturation. Repeating the cycle many times (for example 30) amplifies the DNA about a billion times: copies after n cycles = starting copies × 2ⁿ.

**Amplification in vivo:** the recombinant vector is introduced into a host where it **replicates** with the help of the **ori**, and multiplies as the host divides; high-copy-number plasmids give many copies per cell. If the gene is expressed in a suitable host, the **recombinant protein** is produced as well.

sections.heading: 6. Bioreactors and downstream processing
sections.body_md:
To produce large quantities of products, cells are grown in **bioreactors**, where large volumes (**100–1000 litres**) of culture can be processed. A bioreactor provides optimal conditions — **temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins and oxygen**.

**Stirred-tank bioreactors** are usually **cylindrical** or have a **curved base** to help mixing. The **stirrer** facilitates even mixing and **oxygen availability** throughout. **Sparged-tank bioreactors** bubble **sterile air** through the medium, which increases the area for oxygen transfer. A bioreactor has an **agitator system**, an **oxygen-delivery system**, a **foam-control system**, a **temperature-control system**, a **pH-control system** and **sampling ports**.

**Downstream processing:** after the biosynthetic stage, the product undergoes **separation and purification**, then is **formulated** with suitable **preservatives**. Drugs undergo thorough **clinical trials**, and strict **quality-control** testing is required for each product.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying DNA moves to the cathode (it is negatively charged and moves to the anode).
- Writing that larger fragments travel farther in a gel (smaller ones do).
- Calling any sequence that reads the same forwards a palindrome; for DNA both strands must read the same 5′→3′.
- Saying recombinants grow on tetracycline after insertion at BamHI (they do not; tetᴿ is inactivated).
- Saying blue colonies are recombinant (white ones are).
- Forgetting that Taq polymerase is used because it is heat-stable.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: an enzyme for lysis, the meaning of a letter in EcoRI, a vector feature, a PCR step.
- 2–3-mark questions: sticky ends; features of vectors; competent cells; insertional inactivation; PCR.
- 5-mark questions in parts: steps of recombinant DNA technology; pBR322 with selection of recombinants; PCR with amplification; bioreactors.

The required band is **cut out** and the DNA extracted from it (**elution**).

Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation for Assertion.
Assertion is true and Reason is false.
Both Assertion and Reason are false.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and reading the same 5′→3′ on both strands is what makes it palindromic — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The enzyme that joins DNA fragments with matching sticky ends into recombinant DNA is DNA ______.

questions.stem_md: A linear DNA whose top strand reads 5′–ACGAATTCTTGAATTCGGAATTCA–3′ is cut completely with EcoRI (site GAATTC). How many fragments are produced?
questions.solution_md: GAATTC occurs 3 times in the linear molecule, so it is cut into $3 + 1 = 4$ fragments.

questions.solution_md: Only GGATCC has a reverse complement (GGATCC) equal to itself; for example, GGATCG gives CGATCC — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Explain how restriction enzymes are named, using EcoRI as an example.

answer.model_answer_md: The **first letter** is from the **genus** and the next **two** from the **species** of the bacterium; the next letter gives the **strain**, and the **Roman numeral** the **order** in which the enzyme was isolated from that strain. **EcoRI**: ***E***scherichia ***co***li, strain ***R***Y 13, the **first** (I) enzyme isolated.

questions.solution_md: Genus, species, strain, order.

questions.stem_md: State three features of restriction endonucleases that make them useful in genetic engineering.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) Each recognises a **specific palindromic sequence** and cuts **only there**, so cuts are **predictable**. (ii) Many cut the two strands **a little away from the centre**, leaving **sticky ends** that **pair with complementary ends** made by the same enzyme. (iii) Because the **same enzyme** gives matching ends on any DNA, fragments from **different sources** (vector and foreign DNA) can be **joined by ligase**.

questions.solution_md: Specificity, sticky ends, compatibility.

marking_scheme.step: Same ends on any DNA; joined by ligase

questions.stem_md: Explain, with the help of a diagram, how EcoRI produces sticky ends and how these are used to make recombinant DNA.

answer.model_answer_md: **Diagram:** the duplex with **GAATTC** on the top strand and **CTTAAG** below; EcoRI cuts **between G and A** on **both** strands, a little away from the centre, leaving **single-stranded AATT overhangs** — **sticky ends**. They are “sticky” because they form **hydrogen bonds** with complementary overhangs. If the **vector** and the **foreign DNA** are cut with **EcoRI**, their ends pair, and **DNA ligase** seals the backbones, producing **recombinant DNA**.

questions.solution_md: Staggered cut; pairing; ligase.

marking_scheme.step: Cut between G and A on both strands
AATT overhangs pair by hydrogen bonds
Vector and insert joined by ligase

questions.stem_md: In blue-white selection, a colony is blue on a plate with a chromogenic substrate. What does this tell you?

questions.stem_md: In a blue-white screen, 120 colonies grew, of which 18 were white. What percentage of colonies were recombinant?
questions.solution_md: White colonies are recombinant: $\dfrac{18}{120} \times 100 = 15$ percent.

questions.stem_md: A plasmid solution is simply mixed with untreated E. coli cells, and almost none of them take up the plasmid. Explain why, and describe how the cells can be made competent.

answer.model_answer_md: DNA is **hydrophilic** and cannot pass through **cell membranes**, so cells must be made **competent**. They are treated with a specific concentration of a **divalent cation, calcium**, incubated with the recombinant DNA **on ice**, given a brief **heat shock at 42 °C**, and returned to **ice**.

questions.solution_md: Hydrophilic DNA; calcium and heat shock.

questions.stem_md: Explain the principle of blue-white selection of recombinants.

answer.model_answer_md: The vector carries the **lacZ** gene for **β-galactosidase**. Foreign DNA is inserted **within lacZ**, **inactivating** it (**insertional inactivation**). On a medium with a **chromogenic substrate**, colonies with an intact lacZ make **blue** colour, while **recombinant** colonies cannot and stay **white**, so they are picked by colour.

questions.solution_md: lacZ inactivation.

questions.stem_md: A student inserts a gene at the BamHI site of pBR322, transforms E. coli and plates the cells on ampicillin, then replica-plates them on tetracycline. Predict which cells grow where, and identify the recombinants.

Cells with the **recombinant** plasmid have **tetᴿ inactivated** by the insert at BamHI, so they grow on **ampicillin but not on tetracycline**. Colonies **missing** from the tetracycline replica are the **recombinants**.

questions.solution_md: $2^{9} = 512 < 1000$ and $2^{10} = 1024 \ge 1000$, so the smallest number of cycles is $n = 10$.

questions.stem_md: A gene can be multiplied by PCR or by cloning in a host. Give two differences between these methods of amplification.

answer.model_answer_md: **PCR** amplifies DNA **in vitro**, in a tube, using **primers and Taq polymerase**, and gives **DNA only**. **Cloning** amplifies it **in vivo**: the vector **replicates inside host cells** using the **ori** and the host’s enzymes, and if the gene is **expressed**, the host also makes the **protein**.

questions.solution_md: In vitro vs in vivo.

questions.stem_md: Describe the three steps of a PCR cycle and explain why the amount of DNA doubles each cycle.

answer.model_answer_md: **Denaturation:** high temperature separates the double-stranded DNA into **single strands**. **Annealing:** at a lower temperature, two **primers** bind to complementary sites flanking the target. **Extension:** the **thermostable Taq polymerase** adds nucleotides to the primers, copying each strand. Since **each strand acts as a template**, every DNA molecule gives **two** in each cycle, so copies **double** (2ⁿ after n cycles).

questions.solution_md: Three steps; doubling.

(b) How many copies would 2 starting molecules give after 15 cycles? [1]
(c) State one use of PCR. [1]

(a) **Diagram:** double-stranded DNA → **denaturation** (high temperature; strands separate) → **annealing** (two **primers** bind to complementary ends of the target) → **extension** (**Taq polymerase**, heat-stable, from *Thermus aquaticus*, adds nucleotides) → **two** double-stranded copies; the cycle is **repeated**.

(b) $2 \times 2^{15} =$ **65536** copies.

(c) Amplifying a **gene for cloning**, **early diagnosis** of infections (detecting very low numbers of a pathogen), or **DNA fingerprinting** from tiny samples.

questions.solution_md: Cycle; copies; use.

questions.stem_md: What is downstream processing, and why are clinical trials and quality control part of it for drugs?

answer.model_answer_md: **Downstream processing** is the **separation and purification** of the product after the biosynthetic stage, followed by **formulation** with suitable **preservatives**. For drugs, **clinical trials** and strict **quality control** ensure the product is **safe and effective** before it is marketed.

questions.solution_md: Definition; safety.

questions.stem_md: List the systems that a bioreactor must have and explain why such control is needed for large-scale production.

answer.model_answer_md: A bioreactor has an **agitator** system, an **oxygen-delivery** system (sparger), a **foam-control** system, a **temperature-control** system, a **pH-control** system and **sampling ports**. These keep **optimal conditions** — temperature, pH, substrate, salts, vitamins and oxygen — so that the desired cells grow **rapidly and uniformly** in **100–1000 litres** and produce the **maximum product** without contamination.

questions.solution_md: Systems; optimal conditions.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram of a stirred-tank bioreactor. [2]
(b) How does a sparged-tank bioreactor differ from it? [1]
(c) Why must the medium and air supplied to a bioreactor be sterile? [1]
(d) Why is the product passed through downstream processing before sale? [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diagram:** a **cylindrical vessel** with a **curved base**; a **motor-driven impeller (agitator)**; a **sterile-air inlet (sparger)** at the bottom; a **foam breaker** and **exhaust**; a **temperature-control jacket**; **pH probe** and **sampling port**.

(b) In a **sparged tank**, **sterile air bubbles** do the mixing and aeration, increasing oxygen transfer, instead of a strong impeller.

(c) **Contaminating microbes** would compete with the desired cells, spoil the product and could be **harmful**; bioprocess engineering requires **sterile** conditions.

(d) The product must be **separated, purified** and **formulated** (with preservatives), and drugs must pass **clinical trials and quality control**.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
A gene was ligated into the BamHI site of pBR322 and the mixture was used to transform competent E. coli. Colonies from an ampicillin plate were replica-plated onto a tetracycline plate.

| Colony | Grows on ampicillin | Grows on tetracycline |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Yes | Yes |
| 2 | Yes | No |
| 3 | Yes | Yes |
| 4 | Yes | No |
| 5 | Yes | Yes |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 2

**(b)** (b) Their plasmids have no insert, so tetᴿ is intact.

**(c)** (i) Most cells in the mixture did not take up any plasmid. These untransformed cells **lack the plasmid**, so they have **no ampᴿ gene** to protect them, and **ampicillin kills** them. The ampicillin plate therefore allows only **transformants** — cells carrying pBR322, with or without an insert — to form colonies.

**OR** (ii) The two-plate method is **cumbersome**: colonies must be **replica-plated** on two media. In blue-white selection, recombinants are recognised **directly by colour** on a **single plate**.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Colonies 2 and 4 grow on ampicillin but not tetracycline: 2 recombinants.

**(b)** Non-recombinant plasmids keep both resistance genes — option (b).

**(c)** (i) No ampᴿ.

(ii) One plate, by colour.

questions.passage_md: A linear DNA with the top strand 5′–GCGAATTCAAAAAAAAAAAAGAATTCTT–3′ was cut with EcoRI (site GAATTC, cut between G and A) and the fragments were run on an agarose gel beside a ladder of known sizes (see the figure).

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 3

**(b)** (a) The shortest fragment, GCG

**(c)** (i) The ladder contains fragments of **known size**, which form reference bands. Because all lanes run under the **same conditions**, the **distance moved** by each unknown band can be compared with the ladder bands, and its **size estimated** by interpolation between them.

**OR** (ii) The gel is stained with **ethidium bromide** and viewed under **UV light**, showing **orange bands**. The required band is **cut out** and the DNA **extracted** from the gel piece (**elution**).

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Two sites in a linear molecule give 3 fragments: GCG, AATTCAAAAAAAAAAAAG, AATTCTT.

**(b)** Smaller fragments pass through the agarose sieve faster — option (a).

**(c)** (i) Reference for size.

(ii) EtBr, UV, elution.
